paper.title: How simple can you go? An off-the-shelf transformer approach to molecular dynamics
paper.file_name: 32_How simple can you go - An off-the-shelf transformer approach to molecular dynamics.pdf
paper.research_summary: This paper presents MD-ET, a minimally modified edge transformer architecture for molecular dynamics (MD) that intentionally omits built-in rotational equivariance and energy conservation—two common physical inductive biases in neural MD models. Trained on ∼30 × 10⁶ structures from the QCML database via supervised pretraining, MD-ET achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks after few-shot fine-tuning. The study evaluates how well an 'off-the-shelf' transformer can learn approximate equivariance and energy conservation purely from data, and assesses its ability to perform stable NVE and faithful NVT MD simulations.

tasks.task_name_raw: molecular dynamics simulation using a neural network force field
tasks.objective: To develop and evaluate a neural network force field for molecular dynamics simulation that relies minimally on architectural physical inductive biases (e.g., built-in rotational equivariance or energy conservation), instead learning approximate physical consistency from data.
constraints: no automatic differentiation of energy to obtain forces
output_goal: stable molecular dynamics trajectories (NVE and NVT ensembles)

evidence.text: We present a recipe for MD using an edge transformer (ET), an “off-the-shelf” transformer architecture that has been minimally modified for the MD domain, termed MD-ET. Our model implements neither built-in equivariance nor energy conservation.

We thus study an extreme case: we present and evaluate the best MD model we can build using a minimal amount of MD-specific design features. Specifically, we aim to use an architecture that could be used in some related ML setting with minimal changes.

stages.stage_goal: Obtain a large-scale quantum chemistry reference dataset spanning the periodic table, including out-of-equilibrium structures and different spin and charge states.

evidence.text: QCML ranges across the periodic table, including out-of-equilibrium structures and different spin and charge states, and includes properties for a subset of ∼30 × 10⁶ entries calculated with density functional theory accuracy at the PBE0 level46,47 (including dispersion corrections48,49).
evidence.section: We examine the effects of forgoing almost all commonly

stages.stage_goal: Partition QCML into train/validation/test splits while preserving conformational grouping, and apply random rotations and reflections to enable learning of approximate O(3)-equivariance.

evidence.text: We create an approximate 90%/5%/5% split from QCML. As QCML contains multiple conformations for each structure sampled along its normal modes, we ensure that all conformations of a structure are assigned to the same split.
To learn approximate equivariance, we use data augmentation: during pretraining, we duplicate each batch once and apply random rotations and reflections to both copies to form an augmented batch.

stages.stage_name_raw: supervised pretraining of MD-ET on QCML
stages.stage_goal: Train the MD-adapted edge transformer (MD-ET) to predict atomic forces directly (not via energy gradients) using mean absolute error loss on QCML.
stage_input: MD-ET architecture with MD-specific embedding layers

evidence.text: We perform supervised pretraining on the new QCML dataset.45 [...] During training, we use two randomly rotated and mirrored copies of each sampled structure so that our model can learn approximate O(3)-equivariance. Instead of predicting a combined loss50 of energies and forces or calculating forces as the negative gradient of the predicted energy with respect to positions, we predict forces directly.

evidence.text: We train MD-ET for 880k steps on QCML using a batch size of 1024 (i.e., 512 before data augmentation), which takes ∼16 A100 GPU-days

stages.stage_name_raw: benchmark evaluation on standard MD datasets
stages.stage_goal: Assess pretrained MD-ET’s zero-shot and few-shot performance across diverse MD benchmarks (QCML, MD17, Ko2020, xxMD, SPICE) measuring force MAE, simulation stability, faithfulness (h(r)), and inference speed.
stage_output: benchmark scores (MAE, stability time, h(r), FPS)

evidence.text: We evaluate the performance of our proposed MD-ET model across several standard MD benchmarks. We compare MD-ET with established MLFFs, focusing on their accuracy, stability, and efficiency. We evaluated MD-ET on QCML,45 MD17,15 Ko2020,67 xxMD,68 and SPICE,69 each presenting distinct challenges.
For MD simulations, we evaluate either the pretrained model without further training (zero-shot) or fine-tune using a small number of samples of the target structure (few-shot).

stages.stage_name_raw: quantitative analysis of equivariance and energy conservation
stages.stage_goal: Compute equivariance error E_eq and antisymmetric ratio λ (Jacobian symmetry metric) to quantify how closely MD-ET approximates rotational equivariance and energy conservation.

evidence.text: Bigi et al.29 examine the Jacobian matrix of the force prediction with respect to atom positions J ∈R3n×3n to quantify energy conservation. The Jacobian of a perfectly energy-conserving prediction should be a symmetric matrix since it is the Hessian of the molecular energy. Bigi et al.29 quantify the symmetry of J by decomposing the matrix into its symmetric and antisymmetric components and calculating the ratio between the Frobenius norm of the antisymmetric component and the Frobenius norm of the entire matrix, i.e., λ = ∥Janti∥F / ∥J∥F

stages.stage_name_raw: NVE and NVT molecular dynamics simulations
stages.stage_goal: Run and analyze MD simulations (NVE and NVT ensembles) to empirically validate stability, energy conservation, and observables fidelity (e.g., h(r), velocity–velocity autocorrelation spectra, free energy surfaces).
stage_input: molecular structures (e.g., alkanes, n-octane, alanine dipeptide)

evidence.text: We find that NVE simulations with MD-ET are approximately energy-conserving for some small systems, but with increasing system size, the total energy tends to increase with time (see Fig. 3).
evidence.section: C. Unconstrained models can learn to approximately conserve energy without explicit inductive biases

evidence.text: To evaluate the degree to which MD-ET produces faithful MD simulations, we run 1 ns NVT simulations using the stochastic velocity rescaling (SVR or Bussi) thermostat [...] We then produce velocity–velocity autocorrelation spectra from these trajectories (see Fig. 7, top).
evidence.section: D. Unconstrained models are able to reproduce observables in NVT simulations
